subject: psychology
question_text: Define attitude. Discuss the components of an attitude.
answer_text: Attitude is the tendency to react positively or negatively to a person or circumstances and can be defined as state of the mind, a set of views, or thoughts, regarding some topic which have an evaluative feature (positive, negative or neutral quality). Attitude has three components: (i) The thought component is referred to as the cognitive aspect: It consists of belief, ideas, values and other information that a person may possess or has faith in. (ii) The emotional component is known as the affective aspect: It is related to person’s feelings about another person. (iii) The tendency to act is called the behavioural (or conative) aspect: It is related to impact of various situations or objects that lead to individual’s behaviour based on cognitive and affective components.
final_answer: Thus, the three components of attitude are cognitive, affective, and behavioral.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of the concept of attitude and its components.

subject: psychology
question_text: What are the factors that influence the formation of an attitude?
answer_text: Factors that influence the formation of an attitude include characteristics of the existing attitude, source characteristics, message characteristics, and target characteristics.
final_answer: Thus, various internal and external factors play a role in shaping attitudes.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of multiple factors affecting attitude formation.

subject: psychology
question_text: Is behaviour always a reflection of one’s attitude? Explain with a relevant example.
answer_text: Behaviour is not always a reflection of one’s attitude. For example, Richard LaPiere's study showed that a Chinese couple received positive service despite negative attitudes expressed by hotel managers in surveys.
final_answer: Thus, attitudes may not always predict actual behaviour.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding the relationship between attitudes and behaviour with a real-world example.

subject: psychology
question_text: How does social facilitation take place?
answer_text: Social facilitation occurs when the presence of others enhances an individual's performance on tasks. This is influenced by arousal, evaluation apprehension, and the nature of the task.
final_answer: Therefore, social facilitation can lead to improved performance in familiar tasks but may hinder performance in complex tasks.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of social psychology concepts and their applications.

subject: psychology
question_text: Your friend eats too much junk food, how would you be able to bring about a change in her/his attitude towards food?
answer_text: I would like to use the concept of cognitive dissonance proposed by Leon Festinger to bring about a change in her/his attitude towards food. The basic idea is that the cognitive components of an attitude must be ‘consonant’ (opposite of ‘dissonant’), i.e., they should be logically in line with each other. If an individual finds that two cognitions in an attitude are dissonant, then one of them will be changed in the direction of consonance. Here the cognitions are: (i) Junk food is bad for health. (ii) He/she eats too much junk food. Holding these two ideas or cognitions will make him feel that something is ‘out of tune’, or dissonant, in the attitude towards junk food. Therefore, one of these ideas will have to be changed, so that consonance can be attained. In order to remove or reduce the dissonance, my friend must stop eating too much junk foods (change Cognition II). This would be the healthy, logical and sensible way of reducing dissonance.
final_answer: Therefore, my friend must stop eating too much junk food to achieve a healthier attitude towards food.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of cognitive dissonance and its application to change behavior.
